standard.title: Water Cycle
standard.description: identify sources of water and describe key processes in the water cycle, including movement of water through the sky, landscape and ocean; precipitation; evaporation; and condensation
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can describe observable properties of solids and liquids and explain how adding or removing heat energy causes changes of state (AC9S3U04). They can compare properties of soils, rocks and minerals as Earth resources (AC9S3U02). They have not yet connected state changes to the movement of water through the environment as a continuous cycle.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students describe the key processes of the water cycle — evaporation, condensation and precipitation — trace the movement of water through sky, landscape and ocean, and identify sources of water including how First Nations Australians and others understand and manage water resources.

nodes.label: Water exists in different forms and locations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify sources of water in the environment — sky, landscape, ocean, underground — and recognise that water exists as liquid, vapour and solid depending on conditions.
nodes.minimum_width: Students name at least three sources of water in the environment and connect each to a state of water (liquid rain, solid snow/ice, vapour in air).
nodes.typical_width: Students describe where water is found across sky, landscape and ocean, and explain that the same water moves between these locations over time.
wider: Map local water sources — creeks, reservoirs, stormwater drains — and trace where water comes from and where it goes
Explore First Nations Australians' knowledge of water sources and landscape reading (identifying water from topographic and vegetation cues)
Investigate underground water (groundwater, aquifers) as a less visible but important water source

response_modes.reason: Students tend to think of water only in visible, surface forms (rain, rivers, taps). Mapping local water sources and exploring First Nations knowledge of water reading broadens this to include underground, atmospheric and landscape-embedded water — supporting the more complete model needed for the full cycle in Node 5.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Local water source mapping and First Nations knowledge of water reading offer genuine richness grounded in place. The groundwater direction provides a less obvious but important extension that challenges students' tendency to think only of surface water.
success_criteria: Identifies at least three sources of water in the environment across different locations (sky, landscape, underground or ocean)
Connects each source to a state of water (liquid, solid or vapour)

nodes.label: Evaporation — liquid water becomes vapour
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain evaporation as the process by which liquid water becomes water vapour and identify everyday examples of evaporation occurring.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe evaporation using an everyday example (wet washing drying, puddle disappearing) and explain that liquid water becomes water vapour that enters the air.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain that heat energy drives evaporation and identify conditions that speed it up (warmth, wind, exposed surface area), connecting to their prior knowledge of heat energy and state change.
wider: Investigate how evaporation rate changes with temperature and surface area using a simple investigation
Explore how First Nations Australians' knowledge of evaporation is applied to conserve water — covering surfaces to reduce evaporative loss
Connect ocean evaporation to the global scale of the water cycle — most water vapour in the atmosphere comes from the ocean
nodes.hinge_reason: Evaporation is the entry point for the water cycle. Students who do not understand that liquid water becomes invisible vapour — and particularly those who restrict evaporation to heating/drying contexts — cannot correctly explain how water enters the atmosphere or why the cycle operates at all, breaking Node 5 integration.

response_modes.reason: Students often have a narrow concept of evaporation tied to drying or heating — they miss large-scale evaporation from oceans and lakes, and evaporation in cool conditions. Varied everyday examples help students generalise beyond heat-drying to a broader concept of liquid-to-vapour transition.

success_criteria: Describes evaporation using an everyday example and explains that liquid water becomes water vapour
Identifies at least one condition that affects how quickly evaporation occurs

nodes.label: Condensation — vapour becomes liquid water
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain condensation as the process by which water vapour becomes liquid water and identify everyday examples where condensation is visible.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe condensation using an everyday example (water droplets on a cold drink bottle, bathroom mirror fogging) and explain that water vapour in the air becomes liquid water when cooled.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain that cooling drives condensation, connect the formation of clouds to condensation of water vapour in the atmosphere, and describe what conditions are needed for clouds to form.
wider: Observe a 'cloud in a bottle' or fog-formation demonstration and explain the conditions that produced it
Investigate dew formation — when and where does dew form, and why? Connect to First Nations knowledge of collecting dew as a water source
Explore how condensation forms rain droplets — water vapour condenses around tiny particles (dust, pollen) in the atmosphere
nodes.hinge_reason: The condensation misconception (water 'sweats through' a container rather than forming from vapour in the air) directly corrupts students' model of cloud formation and precipitation in Node 4 and Node 5. Students holding this misconception cannot construct a coherent water cycle.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly believe condensation is water 'sweating through' a container rather than water vapour from the air cooling on a cold surface. Making the reasoning explicit — air contains invisible water vapour → cold surface cools nearby air → vapour loses energy and becomes liquid → droplets form on the surface — is necessary before students can correctly explain cloud formation or dew.

success_criteria: Describes condensation using an everyday example and explains that water vapour becomes liquid water when cooled
Does not describe condensation as water passing through a container wall (misconception check)
Connects cloud formation to condensation of water vapour in the atmosphere

nodes.label: Precipitation — water falls from clouds
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain precipitation as water falling from clouds in different forms (rain, snow, hail) and describe the conditions that determine which form precipitation takes.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain that precipitation occurs when water droplets in clouds combine and fall, and name two forms of precipitation.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe conditions that determine precipitation form (temperature at different altitudes determines rain vs snow vs hail) and give examples of each from different climates or seasons.
wider: Explore how rainfall data is collected and used — rain gauges, Bureau of Meteorology data — connecting to how hydrologists use this data (AC9S4H01)
Investigate seasonal rainfall patterns in different Australian regions and connect to First Nations seasonal calendars
Examine hail formation as an example of precipitation with a more complex mechanism — water droplets carried upward by air currents, freezing in layers

response_modes.reason: Students commonly think of precipitation only as rain and miss the variety of forms and the conditions that determine them. Exploring rainfall data collection and First Nations seasonal calendars broadens students' understanding of precipitation as a varied, data-rich phenomenon embedded in real knowledge systems.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Rainfall data collection connects precipitation to AC9S4H01 (how data supports scientific explanations) and to real-world hydrology. First Nations seasonal calendars provide a rich cross-cultural perspective on understanding precipitation patterns.
success_criteria: Explains that precipitation occurs when water falls from clouds and names at least two forms
Describes at least one condition that determines what form precipitation takes

nodes.label: The water cycle — continuous movement through Earth's systems
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can trace the movement of water through the complete cycle — evaporation, condensation, precipitation, runoff and collection — and explain that the water cycle is continuous.
nodes.minimum_width: Students trace a water molecule through at least three stages of the water cycle, naming the processes at each transition and identifying where the water is at each stage.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the complete water cycle including the movement of water through sky, landscape and ocean, explain that solar energy drives the cycle, and represent it in a labelled diagram or model.
wider: Explore how hydrologists use rainfall and water use data to explain river flow and seasonal variation (AC9S4H01) — connecting the abstract cycle to real data
Examine how land use changes (deforestation, urbanisation) affect the water cycle at local and regional scales
Consider how First Nations Australians' water resource management practices are grounded in understanding the water cycle, including seasonal variation

response_modes.reason: The water cycle integrates evaporation, condensation and precipitation — three processes students have encountered separately — into a single continuous system. Students must now coordinate these components and understand that the same water moves repeatedly through the cycle, driven by solar energy.

Students tend to model the water cycle as a simple loop (rain falls, evaporates, becomes rain again) without accounting for groundwater, ocean reservoirs, or long-term storage in ice. Varied representations — local creek, ocean, underground — help students build a more complete model of the cycle.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Connecting the water cycle to real hydrology data (AC9S4H01) and land use impacts offers substantial enrichment. Students engaging the wider tier can see how an abstract scientific model has direct applications in water resource management — a connection that is meaningful and non-trivial.
success_criteria: Traces the path of water through at least three named stages of the water cycle, correctly labelling the process at each transition
Explains that the water cycle is continuous and driven by solar energy
Identifies at least two locations where water is stored (e.g. ocean, atmosphere, groundwater, ice)
